newsitem.title: USA: Clinton pays holiday visit to elite Marine unit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton pays holiday visit to elite Marine unit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, in a Yuletide salute to the U.S. armed forces, visited a sprawling Marine base on Monday to greet troops on duty over the holidays.

Clinton, on his first domestic trip since his re-election on Nov. 5, was in his commander-in-chief role in his visit to Camp Lejeune, a 230-square-mile (595 square km) complex in eastern North Carolina where some 42,000 Marines and sailors are based.

A highlight of Clinton's 4 1/2-hour stay at the headquarters of Marine Forces Atlantic was lunch with members of the Air Contingency Force, a rapid reaction unit prepared to spring into action with as little as four hours notice should an international crisis erupt.

These elite troops are on standby alert over Christmas and New Years' Day and cannot go home for the holidays. Some of those who dined with the president took part in emergency operations to protect American citizens in Liberia and the Central African Republic last summer.
Their unit also participated in the daring rescue of downed Air Force pilot Scott O'Grady from Serbian-controlled territory in Bosnia in 1995.

Clinton, who will spend his fourth Christmas at the White House on Wednesday, also made time for a visit with volunteer social service workers, many of them spouses of Marines and sailors posted overseas. He planned to complete his visit with a holiday speech at a base gymnasium.

The White House said the president had chosen the Marines to represent the men and women of all of the armed forces, and had come to thank them on behalf of the American people "for the sacrifices they make to maintain the safety and security" of the United States."

Clinton was also mindful of the fact that Camp Lejeune was the scene of a mid-air collision between two military helicopters that killed 12 Marines last spring, and that it was hard hit by two hurricanes -- Bertha and Fran -- last summer.
The storms hit when many of the troops were on temporary duty abroad, and "many of them have come home to some pretty heavy yardwork," a Marine spokesman said.

But there was also a 2-year-old political sub-plot to Clinton's visit. In 1994, conservative North Carolina Sen. Jesse Helms, a fierce critic who is especially disdainful of Clinton for avoiding military service during the Vietnam War, said the president was so unpopular among the troops that he could not safely visit a military base in Helm's state.
"Mr. Clinton better watch out if he comes down here. He'd better have a bodyguard," Helms said in a November 1994 interview. He later said the bodyguard remark was not meant literally.
